evidence: ProjectController.ts: class ProjectController with `readonly router = Router()`; its handlers `create` and `list` call CreateProjectUseCase.execute and ListProjectsUseCase.execute, and input is read via asFields/requiredString(body, 'name')

TaskController.ts: class TaskController registers add/list/assign/complete routes; every input is read through asFields, requiredString and optionalString from '../requestFields' (e.g. requiredString(asFields(req.params), 'taskId'))

UserController.ts: class UserController follows the same router/constructor-injection/handler structure and calls CreateUserUseCase and ListUsersUseCase, with input read via requiredString(body, 'name')
Validation logic is not re-implemented in any controller; all three import from src/infrastructure/http/requestFields.ts
Each controller is wired by its own composition module (projectModule.ts, taskModule.ts, userModule.ts)
parsedVerdict.reasoning: All three files do one job: they are Express HTTP controllers that map requests to application use cases. Each one follows the same pattern. It exposes a `readonly router = Router()`, receives its use cases through the constructor, registers its routes in the constructor, and uses private arrow-function handlers that call `useCase.execute(...)` and return JSON. All request parsing goes through the shared `requestFields` helpers (`asFields`, `requiredString`, `optionalString`), so the parsing and validation rules live in one place and no controller reads `req.body`, `req.params` or `req.query` fields directly. No controller holds business rules. `TaskController` does default `description` to an empty string, but that is input mapping that only it does, not a rule repeated elsewhere. `ProjectController` and `UserController` are shaped alike, but that is the same pattern applied to two resources, not a duplicated invariant.
